title: Mother of man killed by police joins call for inquiry into systemic racism
article: The mother of Jon Wells joined Assembly of First Nations (AFN) chiefs Wednesday in calling for a national inquiry into systemic racism in policing.
The 42-year-old Blood Tribe member died during a Sept. 17 interaction with Calgary police officers at a city hotel.

The Alberta Serious Incident Response Team (ASIRT), which continues to investigate the incident, has said the unarmed man repeatedly told officers he did not want to die before being punched and Tased.
Roy Fox, then the Blood Tribe chief, called for a public inquiry into Wells' death.
"At this time I just want to say that justice needs to be done, and what they have done to him, that was racism," Edith Wells said during a press conference Wednesday in Ottawa.
"I'm just so hurt, devastated, and I'm shattered."
Other grieving First Nations mothers need to speak up for justice for their children, said Wells.
"It is really hard, but I have to stand here and talk on his behalf to be heard."
Since August, 13 First Nations people have reportedly died following police interactions, said Terry Teegee, regional chief for the British Columbia Assembly of First Nations on Wednesday.
A national inquiry should be held not only into the deaths of Indigenous people during police interactions but also into a policing system he called "inherently racist."
"This is really important that this is highlighted on the highest level, that there needs to be systemic change in policing," said Teegee.
AFN National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak called the situation a "black eye" for Canada that's unacceptable to First Nations people as well as other Canadians.
"We have many allies out there, and they're horrified when we talk about this issue," said the national AFN chief, who called for the public inquiry to take place immediately.
Gabriel Brunet, spokesperson for Public Safety Minister Dominic LeBlanc, did not specifically answer Postmedia's question about whether LeBlanc supported an inquiry.

Since 2018, Canada has invested significantly to bolster the First Nations and Inuit Policing Program to further increase access to dedicated, culturally responsive policing services in First Nations communities, said Brunet.

"We recognize that recent officer-involved fatal incidents in Indigenous communities have been incredibly difficult for community members, and most of all (for) the loved ones of the deceased. Our thoughts are with them," said Brunet.
LeBlanc recently met with Woodhouse Nepinak to discuss how they can work together to ensure policing in Canada is "responsive and respectful."
"There is still a lot of work to be done, but we will get there through ongoing collaboration and frank, open dialogue," said Brunet.
